definition:
Hell is the Bible's name for the final destiny of those who, at the last judgment, are shut out from the life of God's kingdom. Scripture describes it in several images that do not fit neatly together: fire that is not quenched, outer darkness with weeping and grinding of teeth, destruction of body and soul, exclusion from the presence of the Lord, a lake of fire called the second death. What the images share is loss: the loss of the life, light, and fellowship with God for which human beings were made. Jesus spoke of it more often and more sharply than anyone else in Scripture, and the church has always confessed that it is real, just, and in the hands of the God revealed in Christ. How it is to be understood, as unending conscious punishment, as final destruction, or (for a minority) as a punishment that may finally give way to restoration, is the question on which Christians differ.

English Bibles once used the one word ‘hell’ for several different terms, which has confused many readers. Sheol, the Hebrew word for the grave or the realm of the dead, appears about sixty-five times in the Old Testament; it is where all the dead go, righteous and wicked alike, and the Greek translation of the Old Testament usually renders it hadēs. In the New Testament Hades (ten times) is likewise mostly the realm of the dead between death and resurrection, and at the end it is itself thrown into the lake of fire (Revelation 20:14); that waiting condition is treated in its own study (Death and the Intermediate State). The word that properly means the final hell is geenna, Gehenna, from the Hebrew ge hinnom, ‘the Valley of Hinnom’, the ravine on the south side of Jerusalem where kings of Judah had burned children in sacrifice (2 Kings 16:3; 21:6; Jeremiah 7:31). It appears twelve times in the New Testament, eleven of them on Jesus' lips and once in James 3:6. Second Peter 2:4 uses once the verb tartaroō, ‘to cast into Tartarus’, borrowing the Greek poets' name for the deepest pit of the underworld, for the imprisonment of the angels who sinned. The adjective aiōnios, usually translated ‘eternal’, means ‘belonging to the age’, that is, to the age to come; in the New Testament it describes both the life of the saved and the punishment of the lost (Matthew 25:46), and what it implies about duration is one of the points of debate. Other key words are kolasis, ‘punishment’ (Matthew 25:46), olethros, ‘ruin’ or ‘destruction’ (2 Thessalonians 1:9), and apōleia, ‘destruction’ or ‘perishing’ (Matthew 7:13).
ot:
The Old Testament says little directly about a final hell. Its horizon for most of its history is Sheol, and its warnings concern judgment in this life: exile, defeat, death. But the ground is laid in three ways. The first is exclusion from God's presence. After the first sin God “banished him from the Garden of Eden” and set cherubim and a flaming sword “to guard the way to the tree of life” (Genesis 3:23-24). Life was found in God's presence, and to be driven from it was to be cut off from life. The second is fire as the instrument of God's judgment on settled wickedness. The LORD “rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah” (Genesis 19:24), and the New Testament later takes Sodom as an example “of those who sustain the punishment of eternal fire” (Jude 1:7). The prophets speak of God himself as a fire that sinners cannot live beside: “Who of us can dwell with a consuming fire? Who of us can dwell with everlasting flames?” (Isaiah 33:14). Isaiah describes the judgment of Edom as a land whose fire “will not be quenched” and whose “smoke will ascend forever” (Isaiah 34:10), language of permanent desolation that Revelation will reuse (Revelation 14:11; 19:3). Malachi says the wicked will be stubble set ablaze and “ashes under the soles of your feet” (Malachi 4:1-3).

The third is the Valley of Hinnom itself. Kings Ahaz and Manasseh sacrificed their sons there (2 Kings 16:3; 21:6), and King Josiah defiled its shrine, Topheth, so that no one could use it again (2 Kings 23:10). Jeremiah announced that the place of child sacrifice would become “the Valley of Slaughter”, filled with the corpses of the people who had worshiped there (Jeremiah 7:31-33). A place of the worst idolatry would become a place of judgment. The popular idea that the valley was a perpetually burning garbage dump in Jesus' day has no ancient evidence behind it; it is first found in the commentary of the Jewish scholar David Kimhi on Psalm 27, written around AD 1200. The valley's meaning came from Jeremiah, not from rubbish fires.

Two late passages move toward a final state. The last verse of Isaiah pictures worshipers from all nations going out from the new Jerusalem to “see the corpses of the men who have rebelled against Me; for their worm will never die, their fire will never be quenched, and they will be a horror to all mankind” (Isaiah 66:24). Daniel 12:2 speaks of the resurrection of many, “some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt.” The Hebrew word translated ‘horror’ in Isaiah and ‘contempt’ in Daniel, derāʾôn, occurs only in these two verses, which suggests that Daniel was reading Isaiah. Neither says in detail what the condition is: Isaiah speaks of corpses, Daniel of risen people under lasting disgrace, and interpreters of every view find support here. In the centuries between the Testaments Jewish writers developed the picture further. The book of 1 Enoch (chapter 27) describes an accursed valley for the ungodly near Jerusalem, Judith 16:17 speaks of fire and worms in the flesh of the nations that attack Israel, and 4 Ezra, written about AD 100, sets the furnace of Gehenna opposite the paradise of delight at the judgment (4 Ezra 7:36). Jewish views were not uniform: some texts expected the wicked to be destroyed, others to suffer lastingly, and the Mishnah later records Rabbi Akiva's view that the judgment of the wicked in Gehenna lasts twelve months (m. Eduyot 2:10).
nt:
Almost everything the Bible says about Gehenna comes from Jesus, and he speaks of it not to curious outsiders but mostly to his own disciples and to religious leaders. In the Sermon on the Mount, contempt for a brother makes one liable “to the fire of hell” (Matthew 5:22), and it is better to lose an eye or a hand “than for your whole body to be thrown into hell” (Matthew 5:29). He tells his disciples not to fear those who can kill only the body, but to “fear the One who can destroy both soul and body in hell” (Matthew 10:28). In Mark he quotes the last verse of Isaiah: it is better to enter life maimed than to go “into hell, into the unquenchable fire” where “their worm never dies, and the fire is never quenched” (Mark 9:43, 48). He speaks of the ‘outer darkness’, “where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 8:12; 22:13; 25:30), of the broad way “that leads to destruction” (Matthew 7:13), and he asks the Pharisees, “How will you escape the sentence of hell?” (Matthew 23:33). In the parable of the sheep and the goats the King says, “Depart from Me, you who are cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels”, and the scene ends, “And they will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:41, 46). The fire was prepared for the devil, not first for human beings. Jesus also teaches degrees: the servant who knew his master's will receives many blows, the one who did not, few (Luke 12:47-48), and judgment will be more bearable for Sodom than for towns that saw his works (Matthew 11:24). The story of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31) pictures the rich man “in agony in this fire” in Hades with a “great chasm” fixed between him and Abraham; it concerns the time before the resurrection, and interpreters differ on how far a parable's scenery should be pressed, but its point is the finality of the choices made in this life.

The apostles rarely use the word Gehenna; they speak of wrath, death, destruction, and perishing. Paul warns of “wrath and anger” and “trouble and distress for every human being who does evil” (Romans 2:8-9), says “the wages of sin is death” (Romans 6:23), and writes of enemies of the cross whose “end is destruction” (Philippians 3:19). His fullest statement is that when the Lord Jesus is revealed in blazing fire, those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel “will suffer the penalty of eternal destruction, separated from the presence of the Lord and the glory of His might” (2 Thessalonians 1:9). The Greek preposition behind ‘separated from’ can mean either exclusion from the Lord's presence or destruction that comes from his presence, and translators divide. Hebrews warns of “a fearful expectation of judgment and of raging fire that will consume all adversaries” (Hebrews 10:27). John's Gospel frames everything by the alternative of perishing or eternal life (John 3:16) and says the wrath of God remains on the one who rejects the Son (John 3:36). Second Peter and Jude speak of rebellious angels held in darkness for judgment (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 1:6) and of Sodom as an example of eternal fire (Jude 1:7).

Revelation gives the final picture. Those who worship the beast will be “tormented in fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and of the Lamb”, and “the smoke of their torment rises forever and ever” (Revelation 14:10-11). The beast and the false prophet are thrown alive into the lake of fire (Revelation 19:20), and the devil joins them, where “they will be tormented day and night forever and ever” (Revelation 20:10). Death and Hades are thrown in, and “This is the second death—the lake of fire” (Revelation 20:14), along with anyone whose name is not in the book of life. In the new creation, the cowardly, the murderers, the idolaters, and all liars have their place “in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur” (Revelation 21:8), while the city's gates stand open and “outside are the dogs, the sorcerers, the sexually immoral, the murderers, the idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood” (Revelation 22:15). Alongside these warnings stand texts of wide hope, which every view must also read: God's purpose to reconcile “all things” through the blood of the cross (Colossians 1:20), the promise that “in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22), the day when “every knee should bow” (Philippians 2:10), and God “who wants everyone to be saved” (1 Timothy 2:4). The disagreements described below are largely disagreements over how these two sets of texts fit together. The site's survey of the debate is at /theology/doctrine/last-things.

keyTexts.why: The Old Testament's clearest picture of a final fate: the undying worm and unquenched fire over the corpses of rebels, set beside the new heavens and new earth. Jesus quotes it in Mark 9:48.
The resurrection of many, some to everlasting life and others to everlasting contempt. Resurrection and final destiny are joined for the first time.
The Valley of Hinnom, where children were burned in sacrifice, is to become the Valley of Slaughter. The name Gehenna carries this memory of idolatry and judgment.
Jesus tells his disciples to fear the one who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna. The verse is central for both the traditional view and conditional immortality.
The eternal fire was prepared for the devil and his angels, and the scene ends with eternal punishment set beside eternal life, the parallel on which much of the debate turns.
Jesus quotes Isaiah 66:24 about the worm that never dies and the fire never quenched, and calls for radical renunciation of sin rather than speculation.
The servant who knew his master's will receives many blows and the one who did not, few. Judgment is proportioned to knowledge and responsibility.
The rich man and Lazarus pictures conscious suffering in Hades and a fixed chasm. It concerns the time before the resurrection and stresses the finality of this life's choices.
The alternative to eternal life is perishing, and the one who does not believe stands condemned already. The warning is framed inside God's love for the world.
Every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus is Lord. Universalists read this as final reconciliation; others as universal acknowledgment, willing or unwilling.
Those who do not know God will suffer eternal destruction away from the presence of the Lord. Paul's fullest description joins judgment to the vindication of the persecuted.
Rebellious angels are held for judgment, and Sodom serves as an example of eternal fire. The verse shows how the New Testament draws on Genesis for its images.
The smoke of the torment of those who worship the beast rises forever and ever, echoing Isaiah 34:10. Traditionalists and conditionalists read the echo differently.
The devil is tormented forever, Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, and those not in the book of life follow. The lake is called the second death.

history:
Most early Christian writers taught that the punishment of the wicked is unending. Justin Martyr, in his First Apology (about 155), told the emperor that the wicked would be punished in eternal fire, not for the limited period Plato had imagined, and Irenaeus of Lyons taught the same against the Gnostics. Other voices differed. Arnobius of Sicca, early in the fourth century, denied that the soul is naturally immortal and held that the wicked would finally be consumed, the first clear statement of what is now called conditional immortality. Origen of Alexandria (about 185 to 254), in On First Principles, speculated about an apokatastasis, a final restoration of all rational creatures to God, though scholars debate how firmly he held it; Gregory of Nyssa (about 335 to 395) is widely read as hoping for the restoration of all. Augustine answered those he called the merciful, who hoped that punishment would end in book 21 of The City of God (about 426), arguing that since Matthew 25:46 uses the same word ‘eternal’ for punishment and for life, the one cannot end if the other does not. His view became the Western consensus. In 543 an edict of Emperor Justinian and a synod at Constantinople condemned the teaching that the punishment of the wicked will end, and anathemas against Origenist teaching are associated with the Second Council of Constantinople in 553, though historians debate whether the council itself formally adopted them. The Athanasian Creed and the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) confessed eternal punishment for the wicked and eternal glory for the righteous. Dante's Inferno, written in the early fourteenth century, shaped the popular imagination of hell for centuries far beyond anything the creeds said.

The Reformation churches kept the traditional doctrine. The Augsburg Confession (1530, Article 17) condemns those Anabaptists who taught that the punishment of the damned and the devils will come to an end, and the Westminster Confession (1646, chapter 33) says the wicked will be cast into eternal torments and punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord. Jonathan Edwards's sermon Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God (1741) became the most famous English-language sermon on the subject. In the Eastern churches, Isaac the Syrian, a seventh-century bishop and monk, taught that the torment of hell is the experience of God's love by those who have set themselves against it, an idea that has remained influential in Orthodox thought.

From the nineteenth century the traditional view was challenged more openly. Friedrich Schleiermacher leaned toward universal restoration, F. D. Maurice lost his professorships at King's College London in 1853 after his Theological Essays questioned endless punishment, and in America a Universalist church movement grew up that later merged with the Unitarians (1961). Karl Barth's doctrine of election in Christ led him to refuse either to affirm or to deny universal salvation. C. S. Lewis, in The Problem of Pain (1940) and The Great Divorce (1945), described hell as the state of those who will not have God, whose doors are locked from the inside. Among evangelicals, Edward Fudge's The Fire That Consumes (1982) and John Stott's tentative case in Essentials (1988, with David Edwards) revived conditional immortality, and in 2000 the Evangelical Alliance in Britain concluded in its report The Nature of Hell that it is a significant minority evangelical view on which evangelicals may differ. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992) describes hell as definitive self-exclusion from communion with God, whose chief pain is eternal separation from him. Hans Urs von Balthasar's Dare We Hope That All Men Be Saved? (German 1986 and 1987) defended the permission to hope, and David Bentley Hart's That All Shall Be Saved (2019) argued for universalism as certain; both provoked wide debate.

differ.body: The historic majority view, held by the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, and most evangelical churches, is that the lost will exist forever under God's just judgment, consciously and without end. Defenders point to Matthew 25:46, where ‘eternal punishment’ stands beside ‘eternal life’ in one sentence; to the torment that rises ‘forever and ever’ in Revelation 14:11 and 20:10, where the devil, the beast, and the false prophet share one fate with those who follow them; and to the weeping and gnashing of teeth, which describe persons, not ashes. They argue that sin against an infinitely holy God is infinitely serious, that the lost remain rebels, and that the doctrine has the weight of the church's consistent teaching since Augustine and the confessions of the Reformation. Many add that the fire and darkness are images for real separation from God, whose chief pain is that loss.

Only God has immortality in himself (1 Timothy 6:16), and eternal life is his gift to those in Christ. The lost, after judgment and a punishment proportioned to their sins, will finally perish: they will be destroyed body and soul in Gehenna (Matthew 10:28). Defenders note that the Bible's commonest words for the fate of the wicked are death, destruction, and perishing (John 3:16; Romans 6:23; Philippians 3:19), that Isaiah 66:24 speaks of corpses, and that ‘eternal’ often describes a result that lasts rather than a process that continues, as with ‘eternal redemption’ (Hebrews 9:12) and Sodom's ‘eternal fire’ (Jude 1:7), which burned out long ago. The smoke rising forever echoes Isaiah's picture of Edom's permanent desolation. They hold that the idea of an innately immortal soul came more from Plato than from Scripture. Edward Fudge, John Stott, John Wenham, and Clark Pinnock defended it.

A smaller number, from Origen and Gregory of Nyssa to David Bentley Hart and Robin Parry, hold that hell is real but remedial, and that God's love will finally win every creature. They read the texts of wide hope as meaning what they say: God will reconcile all things (Colossians 1:20), in Christ all will be made alive (1 Corinthians 15:22), every knee will bow and every tongue confess Jesus as Lord, which Scripture elsewhere says no one can do except by the Spirit, and God will be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:28). They argue that aiōnios means ‘of the age to come’ rather than endless and that some older Greek usage gave kolasis a corrective sense. Most confessions reject this as a certainty, and many universalists grant that it goes beyond the church's historic teaching. A related position, the hope without certainty set out by Hans Urs von Balthasar, affirms that hell is a real possibility for every person while holding that Christians may pray and hope that no one finally chooses it.

differ.view: The fire and darkness: literal or figurative
differ.body: Within the traditional view Christians also differ over how to read the images. Some, such as John Walvoord, took the fire as a real, physical fire suited to resurrected bodies. Others, such as William Crockett, argue that the biblical writers used fire, darkness, worms, and gnashing of teeth as figures for a real and terrible loss, noting that fire and outer darkness cannot both be literal at once and that the Bible's other pictures of the end are also figurative. Both hold that the reality is more serious, not less, than the images convey. The Orthodox tradition, following Isaac the Syrian, often speaks of the same fire of God's presence being light to those who love him and torment to those who hate him.

errors:
Several popular ideas are not what the church has taught. Hell is not the devil's kingdom, where he rules and punishes sinners; Scripture says the eternal fire was “prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41) and that the devil himself is thrown into it (Revelation 20:10). The medieval pictures of demons with pitchforks, like Dante's precise geography of torments, belong to art and literature, not to the creeds. Luke 16 is not a map of the final state; it concerns Hades before the resurrection and is told to make a point about wealth and repentance. Nor should Sheol and Hades, the realm of all the dead, be confused with Gehenna, the final judgment. And the burning garbage dump, often repeated from pulpits, is a medieval guess and not evidence for or against any view.

The church has also resisted distortions on both sides. It has refused to let the doctrine disappear, since Jesus taught it more than anyone and the gospel is rescue from something real; the confessions of the East and West reject universal salvation taught as a certainty, and the Augsburg Confession named it as an error. It has equally rejected the use of hell as entertainment, as a threat to control people, or as something to speak of with satisfaction. God takes “no pleasure in the death of the wicked” (Ezekiel 33:11), and Paul could wish himself cut off from Christ for the sake of his unbelieving kinsmen (Romans 9:3). Christians are also forbidden to pronounce on the final destiny of particular people; that judgment belongs to Christ alone. Finally, the church has rejected the idea that hell shows God to be arbitrary or cruel. Whatever it is, it is just, proportioned to what each person knew and did, and it is the judgment of the one who bore judgment himself for sinners.
life:
The doctrine of hell tells a person that their life has lasting weight. Choices, loves, and refusals are not erased at death; what a person becomes, they may remain. That is sobering, and it was meant to be. Jesus used these warnings chiefly with his own followers, urging them to cut off whatever leads them into sin and to fear God rather than people. The doctrine also shows the size of the rescue. The gospel is not an improvement plan; it is deliverance from wrath (1 Thessalonians 1:10) through one who entered death himself. Christians who take hell seriously are moved to pray for others and to share the gospel with patience and honesty, not with manipulation or fear tactics.

For many people this doctrine is painful, especially when they think of loved ones who died apart from faith. Scripture does not ask them to pretend otherwise, and it does not give them the right to pronounce on anyone. It does give them the character of the judge: the one who will judge the world is the same Jesus who wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41), who told the thief on the cross he would be with him in paradise, and who will judge each person by what they knew. “Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?” (Genesis 18:25). Believers can leave their dead with him, grieve honestly, and trust that when all is seen, no one will say his judgments were unjust.
questions: Most of what the Bible says about Gehenna comes from Jesus, and much of it is addressed to his own disciples. Why might he have spoken this way to them rather than mainly to outsiders?

Matthew 25:46 sets eternal punishment beside eternal life, while other passages speak of the wicked perishing or being destroyed. How do the traditional view and conditional immortality each explain the other side's texts?
Jesus teaches that judgment is proportioned to what each person knew (Luke 12:47-48). How does that shape the way Christians think about those who never heard the gospel or grieve for loved ones?
